content: DNA amplification can be performed at a single temperature range, unlike PCR, which requires a thermocycler. The detection of amplified DNA products is achieved visually using an ultraviolet (UV) lamp directly within the reaction tubes. This method requires only basic laboratory equipment and can be implemented even in the most resource-limited laboratory settings. However, the current technology does not allow for the detection of mutations in resistance-associated genes. Urinary lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assays, which are biomarker-based tests, currently exhibit suboptimal sensitivity and specificity. As a result, they are not suitable for diagnosing tuberculosis (TB) in all populations. However, these assays demonstrate improved sensitivity for diagnosing TB in individuals co-infected with HIV compared to traditional diagnostic methods. A new class of low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) has been developed for detecting resistance to isoniazid and second-line anti-TB drugs. These tests are intended for use as reflex tests in specimens confirmed to be Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC)-positive. They provide rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) in intermediate and peripheral laboratories. The first product in this class can simultaneously detect resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, and amikacin, with results available in under 90 minutes. This is significantly faster than the current standard of care, which includes line probe assays (LPAs) and culture-based phenotypic DST. Line probe assays (LPAs) are DNA strip-based tests that detect MTBC DNA and determine its drug-resistance profile. They achieve this by analyzing the binding patterns of amplified DNA products (amplicons) to probes targeting specific regions of the MTBC genome, including mutations associated with resistance to anti-TB drugs or the corresponding wild-type DNA sequences. While LPAs are technically more complex than the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, they can detect resistance to a broader range of first-line and second-line drugs and provide mutation-specific data for common variants. These tests are designed for use in reference laboratory settings and are particularly applicable in high TB burden countries. Results can be obtained within five hours. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) represents a new class of diagnostic tests that can detect drug resistance to a wide range of anti-TB drugs. These tests combine the amplification of selected genes with NGS to identify resistance mutations in a single test. Targeted NGS can analyze entire genes to identify specific resistance-associated mutations, potentially offering greater accuracy than existing WHO-recommended diagnostic tests. Additionally, targeted NGS can detect resistance to new and repurposed drugs not currently included in other molecular assays. This technology holds significant potential for providing comprehensive resistance detection tailored to modern treatment regimens. Regulatory approval from national or relevant authorities is required before implementing these new diagnostic tests. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay, developed by Cepheid, marked a significant advancement in improving TB diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection globally. However, its sensitivity is suboptimal, particularly in smear-negative and HIV-associated TB cases. To address these limitations, Cepheid developed the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra), a next-generation assay that uses the same GeneXpert® platform. Xpert Ultra offers improved sensitivity and is recommended as an initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in adults and children with pulmonary TB symptoms. It is preferred over smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic DST due to its higher accuracy and faster results. For adults with pulmonary TB symptoms, Xpert MTB/RIF should be used as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum samples. This recommendation is based on strong evidence for test accuracy and moderate evidence for patient-important outcomes. Similarly, in children with pulmonary TB symptoms, Xpert MTB/RIF should be used as the initial diagnostic test in sputum, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal aspirate, and stool samples. The choice of specimen depends on feasibility and acceptability in the local context. Xpert Ultra is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for adults with pulmonary TB symptoms who have no recent history of TB treatment or a remote history of treatment. It is also recommended for children with pulmonary TB symptoms, with strong evidence supporting its use in sputum samples and lower certainty for other specimen types. For TB meningitis, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as the initial diagnostic test, rather than smear microscopy or culture. This recommendation applies to both adults and children, with moderate evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF accuracy and lower certainty for Xpert Ultra. In cases of extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used in lymph node aspirates, biopsies, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, or urine as the initial diagnostic test. The evidence for test accuracy varies by specimen type, with moderate certainty for pleural fluid and lower certainty for others. For disseminated TB in HIV-positive individuals, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used in blood as the initial diagnostic test. However, this recommendation is based on very low certainty of evidence and applies only to this specific population. Repeat testing with Xpert Ultra is not recommended for adults with pulmonary TB symptoms who have an initial trace-positive result. In children with pulmonary TB symptoms and a negative initial Xpert MTB/RIF result, repeat testing may be considered in settings with a pretest probability of 5% or higher. However, in low-prevalence settings, the benefit of a second test is less pronounced. Clinical judgment and pretest probability should guide treatment decisions, particularly in cases with high pretest probability or uncertain test results. For children living with HIV, recommendations for Xpert MTB/RIF can be extrapolated, but further evidence is needed to evaluate the impact of these tests on outcomes in this population.
